                                             PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                   §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                           §
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION
                                                           §                         OF TEXAS
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                            §



                                    COMMENTS OF
                       GOLDEN SPREAD ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.

         Golden Spread Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“Golden Spread”) submits these comments in
response to the discussion draft (“Discussion Draft”) proposed by the Public Utility Commission
of Texas (“Commission”) Staff (“Staff”) regarding large load interconnection standards. 1 The
Discussion Draft directed comments to be filed by December 19, 2025. These comments are timely
filed.

 I.          BACKGROUND ON GOLDEN SPREAD AND ITS MEMBER COOPERATIVES
         Golden Spread is a not-for-profit electric generation and transmission cooperative with its
principal office in Amarillo, Texas. It supplies cost effective and reliable wholesale electric power
to its sixteen-member not-for-profit distribution cooperatives (“Members”). 2 Golden Spread’s
Members provide retail electric service to approximately 250,000 member-consumers (320,000
meters) in their service areas located over an expansive area, including the Panhandle, South Plains
and Edwards Plateau regions of Texas (covering twenty-four percent (24%) of the Texas, the
Panhandle of Oklahoma, and small portions of Southwestern Kansas and Southeastern Colorado).
Golden Spread’s Members serve consumers in 79 counties. Of those counties, 53 are identified as
rural or remote, as each has fewer than 10,000 inhabitants (2020 Census).



         1
             Staff Discussion Draft, New 16 TAC § 25.194 (Dec. 1, 2025) (“Discussion Draft”).
         2
           Golden Spread’s Members are Bailey County Electric Cooperative Association (Muleshoe, Texas); Big
Country Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Roby, Texas); Coleman County Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Coleman, Texas);
Concho Valley Electric Cooperative, Inc. (San Angelo, Texas); Deaf Smith Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Hereford,
Texas); Greenbelt Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Wellington, Texas); Lamb County Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Littlefield,
Texas); Lighthouse Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Floydada, Texas); Lyntegar Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Tahoka, Texas);
North Plains Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Perryton, Texas); Rita Blanca Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Dalhart, Texas);
South Plains Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Lubbock, Texas); Southwest Texas Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Eldorado,
Texas); Swisher Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Tulia, Texas); Taylor Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Merkel, Texas); and Tri-
County Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Hooker, Oklahoma).

                                                          1
        Figure 1, below, shows the location of Golden Spread’s electric generating units and its
Members’ service territories in Texas and Oklahoma.

             Figure 1. 1 Golden Spread Electric Generating Units and Members' Service Territories




       West Texas has become a focal point for large load development due to the availability of
land, renewable generation, and access to the Electric Reliability Council Of Texas system. In
recent years, Golden Spread’s Members have received a significant volume of interconnection and
service requests from large loads, including data centers and other high demand loads. Golden
Spread and its Members have direct, practical experience navigating the operational, contractual,
and system-planning challenges associated with large load interconnections. Golden Spread’s

                                                      2
 experience with these large loads informs the comments below, which are offered in developing
rules that are workable across utility structures while also advancing the objectives of Senate Bill
(“SB”) 6, enacted in the 89th Regular Session of the Legislature.
       Golden Spread and its Members are members of Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. (“TEC”).
Golden Spread supports the comments of TEC in this docket, and comments separately to
emphasize the issue below.

II.        PRESERVING COOPERATIVE SERVICE RIGHTS WHILE IMPLEMENTING
                  SB 6 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS
       Texas operates under a comprehensive regulatory scheme that includes both competitive
and non-competitive retail service areas served by non-opt-in entities (“NOIEs”), including
electric cooperatives. In non-competitive areas, the NOIE is responsible for providing retail
electric service within its certificated service area, and longstanding statutory mandates prohibit
another utility from furnishing retail electric utility service in an area where service is already
being lawfully furnished, absent appropriate certification. 3 In addition, PURA expressly
recognizes that an electric cooperative that does not offer customer choice retains the right to
provide a full range of customer service and pricing programs to customers within its certificated
retail service area and that other persons or electric utilities may not do so.4
        Golden Spread is concerned that the Discussion Draft’s approach—depending on how
“interconnection utility” is defined and applied—could be interpreted to direct the transmission
owner and operator (i.e., the entity that owns and operates the facilities used to physically
interconnect the large load at transmission voltage) to execute key service agreements with the
large load beyond and inconsistent with that entity’s authority under PURA. That structure would
work in circumstances where the transmission owner and operator is also the entity with the
obligation to provide retail service. However, it does not work uniformly across cooperative
service territories—because many distribution cooperatives do not currently own or operate the
existing transmission facilities that might be used to serve their member-consumers. Under PURA,
though, the distribution cooperative has the legal right to construct, own, and operate new
transmission facilities. In those areas, requiring the transmission owner and operator to execute


       3
           Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA), Tex. Util. Code §§ 37.015(a)-(b).
       4
           PURA §§ 41.052(b), 39.105(b).

                                                         3
 service agreements with the load violates PURA. Such an approach would remove contractual
responsibility from the cooperative that is statutorily authorized and obligated to serve load within
its certificated service area, and instead require contracting and service by an entity that is
statutorily prohibited from doing so.5 SB 6 did not alter PURA’s statutory scheme. The Discussion
Draft, however, would have the effect of doing so, thereby undermining retail service area rights
and obligations.
        Reference to two current statutory/rule provisions illustrates this point. First, PURA §
37.056 grants explicit, sole authority to the entity authorized to provide retail electric service—not
the Transmission Service Provider (“TSP”)—to construct, own, and operate the new transmission
facilities. An excerpt from subsection (f) is as follows:
        … if a new transmission line, whether single or double circuit, will create the first
        interconnection between a load-serving station and an existing transmission facility,
        the entity with the load-serving responsibility or an electric cooperative that has a
        member with a load-serving responsibility at the load-serving station shall be
        certified to build, own, or operate the new transmission line and the load-serving
        station.
Under this provision, a distribution cooperative or a generation and transmission cooperative (like
Golden Spread) that has a member distribution cooperative with the right to provide retail service
has the legal right to construct the line.
        Second, if a TSP or Transmission Distribution Service Provider (“TDSP”) does not have
the legal right to provide retail electric service in the geographic area where the large load is located,
then the TSP/TDSP is prohibited from providing transmission service to the large load. This
restriction is most clearly described in the Commission’s definitions of “transmission service” and
“transmission service customer” in 16 TAC § 25.5. Transmission service is defined as follows:
        Transmission service – Service that allows a transmission service customer to use
        the transmission and distribution facilities of electric utilities, electric cooperatives
        and municipally owned utilities to efficiently and economically utilize generation
        resources to reliably serve its loads and to deliver power to another transmission
        service customer. [Transmission service] [i]ncludes construction or enlargement
        of facilities . . . 6




        5
            PURA §§ 37.015(a)-(b), 37.151, 39.105(b).
        6
            16 TAC § 25.5(140) (emphasis added).


                                                        4
 A transmission service customer is defined to expressly exclude a retail customer. 7 Many TSPs’
delivery tariffs contain the same prohibition.
       In cases where a TSP is “studying” the integration of a retail large load that will need a
new load-serving station, the electric cooperative has the legal right to serve that load and construct
any new facilities required to provide that service, and a TSP is prohibited from doing so. In those
circumstances, the electric cooperative is the transmission service customer of the TSP.
       Golden Spread does not believe the Commission’s objective in implementing SB 6 is to
alter these jurisdictional boundaries or inadvertently undermine cooperative service rights, but the
interconnection standards—including the definition and application of “interconnecting utility”—
need to recognize the roles and responsibilities of different market participants in ERCOT.
       Golden Spread’s state-wide organization, TEC, is proposing its comments to revise the
definition of “interconnecting utility” to include the entity with the right and obligation to serve
the load. Golden Spread believes this change would address its inconsistency with PURA. Golden
Spread also believes that required coordination and information sharing between the transmission
owner/operator and the large load is important to ensure efficient interconnection and accurate
planning. The most appropriate and effective solution will preserve retail service rights and
contracting roles, while also ensuring that the transmission owner/operator remains appropriately
engaged in the coordination process.




       7
           16 TAC § 25.5(141).


                                                  5
                                   III.   CONCLUSION
       Golden Spread appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these comments and looks
forward to working towards a final rule that achieves SB 6’s goals within the parameters of
PURA.

Respectfully submitted,

                                   PROJECT NO. 58481



RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                       §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                              §
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION
                                              §                     OF TEXAS
STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                §


                             EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
                 OF GOLDEN SPREAD ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.

 1) The draft rule’s definition and use of “interconnecting utility” could create jurisdictional
    conflicts if interpreted to require the transmission owner and operator—not the cooperative
    with the certificated retail service obligation—to execute key service agreements with large
    loads. Indeed, if the appropriate roles and responsibilities of market participants are not
    taking into account, then the rules could be inconsistent with existing Commission
    definitions and PURA provisions and encroach on retail electric utilities’ right to serve
    their loads.

 2) Golden Spread supports TEC’s proposed revision to the definition of “interconnecting
    utility,” which would ensure the entity with the right and obligation to serve the load
    remains the contracting counterparty.

 3) Golden Spread agrees that coordination and information sharing with the transmission
    owner (or upstream TSP, as the case may be) remain essential for efficient interconnection
    and system planning, but such coordination must not supplant cooperative service rights or
    contractual authority.
